categories.description: What sound is, how it travels, and how it interacts with tissue

topics.title: Sound Wave Basics
topics.frontClue: Sound needs a medium: it moves energy, not matter, back and forth
topics.corePiece: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave. It carries energy through a medium by making particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction the wave travels; the particles themselves stay in place. Because it is mechanical, sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The wave creates alternating regions of compression (high pressure, high density) and rarefaction (low pressure, low density). The three acoustic variables that change as a wave passes are pressure (pascals), density (kg/cm3), and distance (particle motion). Ultrasound is sound above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), the upper limit of human hearing; infrasound is below 20 Hz. Diagnostic imaging typically uses about 2 to 15 MHz. Seven acoustic parameters describe any wave: period, frequency, amplitude, power, intensity, wavelength, and propagation speed. The first five are set by the sound source. Propagation speed is set only by the medium. Wavelength is the only parameter set by both the source and the medium. When waves meet, in-phase waves add (constructive interference) and out-of-phase waves cancel (destructive interference).
topics.whyLock: SPI loves the question of who determines each parameter, so build that table in your head first and the rest of physics hangs on it. If a question asks what the sonographer can change, the answer is almost always a source parameter, because nobody can change the patient's tissue. Trap: transverse waves, where particles move perpendicular to travel, are not how ultrasound propagates in soft tissue. Trap two: frequency is a parameter, not an acoustic variable. Interference is not just trivia; the random mix of constructive and destructive interference from tiny scatterers is what produces speckle in every gray-scale image.

connectionEdges.title: Frequency, Period & Wavelength
connectionEdges.link: Frequency and period are source-determined parameters, while wavelength depends on both the source and the medium.

connectionEdges.title: Propagation Speed
connectionEdges.link: Speed is the one parameter the medium alone controls, which is why the machine must assume a single value.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions such as which parameter is determined by both source and medium (wavelength), which item is not an acoustic variable, or what lower frequency limit defines ultrasound (20 kHz).

checkpoint.pearl: Source sets period, frequency, amplitude, power, intensity; medium sets speed; both set wavelength
checkpoint.reflection: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum, and which three acoustic variables would you measure to prove a wave is sound?

topics.title: Frequency, Period & Wavelength
topics.frontClue: Reciprocal partners: when one climbs, the other must fall
topics.corePiece: Frequency is the number of cycles per second, measured in hertz; period is the time to complete one cycle, measured in microseconds for diagnostic ultrasound. They are reciprocals: period x frequency = 1, so a 5 MHz wave has a period of 0.2 µs. Both are set by the sound source and cannot be changed by the sonographer except by switching transducers or selecting a different frequency on a broadband probe. Wavelength is the length of one cycle in space: wavelength = propagation speed / frequency. In soft tissue, wavelength in mm = 1.54 / frequency in MHz, so a 2 MHz wave is 0.77 mm long and a 5 MHz wave is about 0.31 mm. Wavelength depends on both the source and the medium. Higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, which produces shorter pulses and better axial resolution, but also more attenuation and therefore less penetration. That resolution versus penetration trade-off is the central decision behind every transducer choice.
topics.whyLock: Many SPI questions are pure proportional reasoning. If frequency doubles, period halves and, in the same medium, wavelength halves. If the beam crosses into a faster medium, frequency stays the same because the source set it, but wavelength lengthens in proportion to the new speed. The classic trap is assuming frequency changes at a boundary; it does not. Memorize 1.54 divided by frequency for soft tissue and check your units: period comes out in microseconds and wavelength in millimeters when frequency is in MHz.

connectionEdges.title: Propagation Speed
connectionEdges.link: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency, so a change in medium changes wavelength even though frequency is fixed.

connectionEdges.title: Axial Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Shorter wavelengths from higher frequencies make shorter pulses and better axial resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Attenuation
connectionEdges.link: Higher frequency improves resolution but attenuates faster, limiting penetration.

topics.registryApplication: Tested both as calculations (period of a 4 MHz wave is 0.25 µs; wavelength of 3 MHz in soft tissue is about 0.51 mm) and as relationships, such as what happens to wavelength when frequency increases or when sound enters bone.

checkpoint.pearl: Frequency up = period down = wavelength down = resolution up = penetration down
checkpoint.reflection: A 5 MHz beam passes from soft tissue into bone. What happens to its frequency, propagation speed, and wavelength?

topics.title: Propagation Speed
topics.frontClue: Stiffness speeds it up, density slows it down; only the medium decides
topics.corePiece: Propagation speed is how fast sound travels through a medium, and it is determined only by the medium's stiffness (bulk modulus, the resistance to compression) and density. Speed is directly related to stiffness and inversely related to density. Stiffness has the larger effect, which is why bone, though dense, is the fastest tissue. Approximate speeds from slowest to fastest: air about 330 m/s, lung about 500 m/s, fat about 1450 m/s, average soft tissue 1540 m/s, liver and blood about 1560 m/s, muscle about 1600 m/s, and bone 2000 to 4000 m/s. Every ultrasound system assumes 1540 m/s, or 1.54 mm/µs, for all tissue. Frequency and amplitude have no effect on speed: all frequencies travel at the same speed in a given medium. The relationship speed = frequency x wavelength holds, but changing frequency simply changes wavelength. The sonographer cannot change propagation speed. The 1540 m/s assumption is what produces the 13 µs per cm rule used to place echoes on the screen.
topics.whyLock: Because the machine assumes 1540 m/s, any tissue with a different speed puts reflectors at the wrong depth. Slower than 1540, as in fat or a silicone implant, means echoes return late and the reflector is drawn too deep; faster means it is drawn too shallow. When the speed change happens at an oblique boundary, the beam also bends. Trap: the controlling word is stiff, not dense. If two media have the same density, the stiffer one is faster; if they have the same stiffness, the denser one is slower. Compressibility is the opposite of stiffness, so more compressible means slower.

connectionEdges.title: Range Equation
connectionEdges.link: The range equation uses the assumed 1.54 mm/µs to convert echo arrival time into depth.

connectionEdges.title: Refraction & Propagation Speed Error
connectionEdges.link: When real speed differs from 1540 m/s, reflectors are misplaced in depth or bent sideways.

connectionEdges.title: Reflection, Impedance & Refraction
connectionEdges.link: Speed is half of acoustic impedance and its change across a boundary is required for refraction.

topics.registryApplication: Typical items ask what determines propagation speed (the medium only), rank media from slowest to fastest, or ask where a reflector will be displayed when the true speed is lower than 1540 m/s.

checkpoint.pearl: Stiffer = faster; denser = slower; more compressible = slower; soft tissue = 1540 m/s
checkpoint.reflection: Media A and B have the same density but A is stiffer. Which carries sound faster, and how would a reflector deep to a slow fatty region be displayed?

topics.title: Amplitude, Power & Intensity
topics.frontClue: Square the amplitude for power; spread power over area for intensity
topics.corePiece: Amplitude is the bigness of a wave: the maximum change of an acoustic variable from its resting value. Peak-to-peak amplitude is twice the amplitude. Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts, and is proportional to amplitude squared. Intensity is the concentration of power in a beam: intensity = power / beam area, measured in W/cm2, so it is also proportional to amplitude squared. If amplitude doubles, power and intensity quadruple. Focusing shrinks beam area, so it raises intensity at the focus without changing total power. All three are set by the source and are adjusted by the sonographer through the output power control (also called transmit power, acoustic power, or energy output). All three decrease as sound travels because of attenuation. Intensity is the parameter most closely tied to bioeffects. Relative changes are expressed in decibels, a logarithmic scale: +3 dB doubles intensity, +10 dB multiplies it by 10, +20 dB by 100; -3 dB halves it and -10 dB reduces it to one tenth.
topics.whyLock: The square relationship is the most common trap: halving amplitude cuts power and intensity to one quarter, not one half. A second trap is focusing, which raises intensity at the focus while total power stays the same. Decibels compare two values, so a dB number means nothing without a starting point, and positive versus negative tells you increase versus decrease. Learn the anchors of 3 dB as a doubling and 10 dB as a tenfold change, and you can solve almost any dB question without a calculator.

connectionEdges.title: Attenuation
connectionEdges.link: Attenuation is the loss of amplitude, power, and intensity, expressed in decibels as sound travels.

connectionEdges.title: Output Power vs Receiver Gain
connectionEdges.link: Output power is the control that changes transmitted amplitude, power, and intensity.

connectionEdges.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
connectionEdges.link: Intensity, especially SPTA, is the key quantity for bioeffects and ALARA decisions.

topics.registryApplication: Expect proportionality questions (amplitude tripled means intensity times 9), the intensity formula, decibel conversions, and which control changes all three (output power).

checkpoint.pearl: Intensity = power / area; power and intensity scale with amplitude squared; 3 dB doubles, 10 dB tenfold
checkpoint.reflection: Output power is lowered until amplitude is half its original value. What happens to intensity, and how many decibels is that change?

topics.title: Attenuation
topics.frontClue: Half a dB per centimeter per megahertz: deeper and higher means weaker
topics.corePiece: Attenuation is the decrease in intensity, power, and amplitude as sound travels through tissue, measured in decibels. It has three components: absorption (sound energy converted to heat, the dominant mechanism in soft tissue), reflection, and scattering. In soft tissue, the attenuation coefficient, the dB lost per cm, is about one half of the frequency in MHz: 0.5 dB/cm/MHz. Total attenuation (dB) = 0.5 x frequency (MHz) x path length (cm), so a 4 MHz beam traveling 6 cm loses about 12 dB. Attenuation increases with higher frequency and with longer distance; propagation speed has no effect on it. The half-value layer thickness is the depth at which intensity falls to one half (a 3 dB loss); it is thin for high frequencies and highly attenuating tissue. Relative attenuation: air and lung are highest, then bone, then soft tissues such as muscle and fat, then blood, and water is lowest. Time gain compensation exists to correct for attenuation so that similar tissues look equally bright at every depth.
topics.whyLock: Attenuation is the penetration half of the frequency trade-off: choose the highest frequency that still reaches the target. It also explains posterior shadowing behind highly attenuating structures and posterior enhancement behind fluid, which barely attenuates. Trap: the attenuation coefficient is per cm and does not depend on distance, but total attenuation grows with distance. Trap two: the half-value layer gets shorter, not longer, as frequency rises. Remember that echoes make a round trip, so the path length for a reflector at depth d is 2d.

connectionEdges.title: Shadowing & Enhancement
connectionEdges.link: Structures that attenuate more or less than surrounding tissue create shadowing or enhancement behind them.

connectionEdges.title: Receiver Functions
connectionEdges.link: Compensation (TGC) is the receiver function built to undo depth-related attenuation.

connectionEdges.title: Frequency, Period & Wavelength
connectionEdges.link: Higher frequency improves resolution but raises the attenuation coefficient proportionally.

topics.registryApplication: Look for calculations using 0.5 dB/cm/MHz, rankings of tissues by attenuation, and identification of absorption as the main source of attenuation in soft tissue.

checkpoint.pearl: Attenuation (dB) = 0.5 x MHz x cm; half-value layer = 3 dB loss
checkpoint.reflection: How much attenuation does a 6 MHz beam experience traveling 2 cm through soft tissue, and why does switching to 3 MHz help deep imaging?

topics.title: Reflection, Impedance & Refraction
topics.frontClue: Mismatch makes echoes; an oblique angle plus a speed change makes bending
topics.corePiece: Acoustic impedance (Z) = density x propagation speed, measured in rayls. Reflection at a boundary with normal (perpendicular) incidence requires an impedance difference, and the larger the mismatch, the stronger the echo. The intensity reflection coefficient = ((Z2 - Z1) / (Z2 + Z1)) squared, and reflected plus transmitted intensity always equals 100 percent. Soft tissue boundaries reflect less than 1 percent; a soft tissue and air boundary reflects about 99.9 percent, which is why gel is needed. Specular reflection occurs at smooth boundaries larger than the wavelength, such as the diaphragm or vessel walls, and is strongly angle dependent. Scattering occurs from structures smaller than the wavelength and creates organ texture; Rayleigh scattering from red blood cells increases with frequency to the fourth power. Refraction is bending of the transmitted beam at an oblique boundary between media of different speeds, described by Snell's law: if medium 2 is faster, the transmission angle is larger than the incidence angle.
topics.whyLock: The two sets of conditions are the heart of this card. Reflection needs an impedance difference. Refraction needs both oblique incidence and different propagation speeds; an impedance difference alone does not bend the beam, and normal incidence never produces refraction. Refraction moves structures sideways on the image and can duplicate them. Specular reflectors are brightest when the beam strikes them at 90 degrees, so an angled diaphragm or tendon can look faint. Rayleigh scattering explains why blood is weakly echogenic but becomes brighter quickly at higher frequencies.

connectionEdges.title: Matching Layer & Backing Material
connectionEdges.link: The matching layer exists to bridge the large impedance gap between the crystal and the skin.

connectionEdges.title: Refraction & Propagation Speed Error
connectionEdges.link: Snell's law bending at oblique boundaries produces lateral displacement and duplication artifacts.

connectionEdges.title: Mirror Image
connectionEdges.link: A strong specular reflector such as the diaphragm creates mirror image artifact.

topics.registryApplication: Questions ask for the conditions needed for reflection versus refraction, which way the beam bends under Snell's law, the impedance formula, and percentages of reflected versus transmitted intensity.

checkpoint.pearl: Reflection needs an impedance mismatch; refraction needs an oblique angle plus a speed change
checkpoint.reflection: Two media have identical impedances but different propagation speeds, struck at an oblique angle. Will there be reflection, refraction, or both?

categories.title: Pulsed Ultrasound
categories.description: Pulse parameters, timing, and axial resolution

topics.title: Pulse Duration & Spatial Pulse Length
topics.frontClue: Fewer cycles and shorter wavelengths make short pulses and sharp detail
topics.corePiece: Pulsed ultrasound sends brief bursts of sound separated by listening time. Pulse duration (PD) is the time the pulse is on: PD = number of cycles in the pulse x period, measured in microseconds, typically 0.5 to 3 µs for imaging. Spatial pulse length (SPL) is the distance the pulse occupies in space: SPL = number of cycles x wavelength, measured in millimeters, typically 0.1 to 1 mm. Both are set by the source; SPL also depends on the medium because wavelength does. The number of cycles is determined by the backing (damping) material: imaging pulses typically contain 2 to 4 cycles, while pulsed Doppler pulses are longer, often 5 to 30 cycles. Higher frequency means shorter period and wavelength, so both PD and SPL shrink. The sonographer cannot change PD or SPL with the depth control; they change only when a different transducer or frequency is selected. Short pulses are desirable for imaging because axial resolution equals one half of the spatial pulse length.
topics.whyLock: PD and SPL describe only the talking part of pulsed ultrasound; PRP, PRF, and duty factor also involve listening time. Students often confuse PD with PRP: PD is the pulse alone, PRP is the pulse plus the listening time. Trap: changing depth changes PRP and PRF but not PD or SPL. Damping, higher frequency, and fewer cycles all shorten the pulse and improve axial resolution. Doppler accepts longer pulses because a narrow bandwidth gives a cleaner frequency shift measurement, at the cost of axial detail.

connectionEdges.title: Axial Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Axial resolution is half the spatial pulse length, so anything that shortens SPL improves it.

connectionEdges.title: PRF & PRP
connectionEdges.link: PRP contains the pulse duration plus listening time, but only the listening time changes with depth.

connectionEdges.title: Bandwidth & Quality Factor
connectionEdges.link: Short, damped pulses contain a wide range of frequencies and therefore a wide bandwidth.

topics.registryApplication: Expect formula and unit questions (SPL = cycles x wavelength), what determines each parameter, and whether the sonographer can change them (not with depth).

checkpoint.pearl: PD = cycles x period; SPL = cycles x wavelength; neither changes with depth
checkpoint.reflection: A 3-cycle pulse at 3 MHz travels through soft tissue. What is its spatial pulse length, and what is its axial resolution?

topics.title: PRF & PRP
topics.frontClue: Deeper imaging means longer listening: PRP rises, PRF falls
topics.corePiece: Pulse repetition period (PRP) is the time from the start of one pulse to the start of the next, and it includes both the pulse duration and the listening time. Pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is the number of pulses sent per second, typically 1 to 10 kHz in imaging. They are reciprocals: PRP x PRF = 1. Listening time, and therefore PRP, is determined by imaging depth, which the sonographer controls. Depth and PRP are directly related; depth and PRF are inversely related. Because each centimeter of depth needs 13 µs of round-trip time, minimum PRP (µs) is about 13 x depth (cm), and maximum PRF (Hz) is about 77,000 / depth (cm). At 10 cm, PRP is about 130 µs and maximum PRF is about 7.7 kHz. PRF is unrelated to the transducer's operating frequency: a 2 MHz probe and a 5 MHz probe imaging to the same depth have the same PRF. A lower PRF limits frame rate and, in pulsed Doppler, lowers the Nyquist limit.
topics.whyLock: PRF is the hub that connects depth, frame rate, and aliasing. Shallow imaging allows a high PRF, faster frames, and a higher Nyquist limit. Deep imaging forces a low PRF so that echoes from one pulse return before the next pulse is sent; when the system breaks that rule, range ambiguity results. Trap: PRF, in kHz, is pulses per second, while operating frequency, in MHz, is cycles per second within the pulse. Trap two: PRP changes with depth but pulse duration does not, so duty factor falls as depth increases.

connectionEdges.title: Range Equation
connectionEdges.link: The 13 µs per cm rule from the range equation sets the minimum PRP for any imaging depth.

connectionEdges.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
connectionEdges.link: The Nyquist limit equals PRF divided by two, so deeper sampling makes aliasing more likely.

connectionEdges.title: Temporal Resolution & Frame Rate
connectionEdges.link: Each scan line takes one PRP, so a longer PRP means fewer frames per second.

topics.registryApplication: Typical items link increased depth to longer PRP, lower PRF, lower frame rate, or more aliasing, and include reciprocal calculations between PRP and PRF.

checkpoint.pearl: Depth up = PRP up = PRF down = Nyquist limit down
checkpoint.reflection: What are the approximate PRP and maximum PRF when imaging to 15 cm in soft tissue?

topics.title: Duty Factor
topics.frontClue: The fraction of time the transducer is talking instead of listening
topics.corePiece: Duty factor, also called duty cycle, is the fraction of time the system is actually transmitting sound: duty factor = pulse duration / pulse repetition period, often multiplied by 100 to express a percentage. It is unitless. Its range is 0 to 1, or 0 to 100 percent: 0 means the system is not transmitting, and 1 (100 percent) means continuous wave ultrasound, which transmits all the time. Clinical pulsed imaging has a very low duty factor, typically about 0.1 to 1 percent, because the system spends more than 99 percent of its time listening for echoes. Pulsed Doppler has a higher duty factor than gray-scale imaging because its pulses contain more cycles. Duty factor is determined by the source, and it changes when the sonographer changes depth: deeper imaging lengthens PRP, so duty factor decreases, while shallower imaging increases it. Duty factor converts between intensities: temporal-average intensity = pulse-average intensity x duty factor. An equivalent formula is duty factor = PD x PRF.
topics.whyLock: Duty factor bridges pulse timing and bioeffects. A higher duty factor delivers more energy over time, so temporal-average intensity rises. Trap: a duty factor of 1.0 is continuous wave, not a very intense pulsed beam. Trap two: depth up lowers duty factor because PD stays fixed while PRP grows. When a question gives PD and PRF instead of PRP, multiply them and watch units: 2 µs x 5 kHz = 2 x 10^-6 s x 5000 per second = 0.01, or 1 percent.

connectionEdges.title: PRF & PRP
connectionEdges.link: PRP is the denominator of duty factor, so depth changes duty factor through PRP.

connectionEdges.title: Pulse Duration & Spatial Pulse Length
connectionEdges.link: Pulse duration is the numerator and is fixed by the transducer, not by depth.

connectionEdges.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
connectionEdges.link: Duty factor converts pulse-average intensities into the temporal-average intensities used in safety.

topics.registryApplication: Tested as calculations, as limits (continuous wave has a duty factor of 100 percent), and as relationships such as what happens to duty factor when imaging depth increases.

checkpoint.pearl: Duty factor = PD / PRP; deeper = lower duty factor; continuous wave = 100 percent
checkpoint.reflection: If pulse duration is 2 µs and PRF is 5 kHz, what is the duty factor, and what happens to it if the sonographer doubles the depth?

topics.title: Range Equation
topics.frontClue: Thirteen microseconds per centimeter: the machine turns time into depth
topics.corePiece: The range equation lets the system calculate reflector depth from the go-return time of an echo: distance to reflector (mm) = propagation speed (mm/µs) x go-return time (µs) / 2. Dividing by two accounts for the round trip. Because the system assumes 1.54 mm/µs in soft tissue, every 13 µs of go-return time corresponds to 1 cm of reflector depth, which is 2 cm of total travel. An echo arriving 26 µs after transmission is placed at 2 cm; one arriving at 130 µs is placed at 10 cm. Depth and time of flight are directly proportional. The same rule sets the minimum PRP for any depth, 13 µs x depth in cm, and therefore the maximum PRF. The range equation relies on assumptions: sound travels in a straight line, at 1540 m/s, reflects only once from structures on the beam axis, and every echo belongs to the most recent pulse. When any assumption fails, artifacts appear, including propagation speed error, reverberation, mirror image, and range ambiguity.
topics.whyLock: This is among the most tested arithmetic on the SPI exam: memorize 13 µs per cm and you can convert in either direction instantly. Trap: forgetting the round trip. If sound travels 10 cm in total, the reflector is 5 cm deep. If the true speed is slower than 1540 m/s, as in fat, echoes arrive late and are drawn too deep; if faster, too shallow. Many artifact questions are range equation questions in disguise, so ask which assumption was broken.

connectionEdges.title: Propagation Speed
connectionEdges.link: The range equation uses the assumed 1540 m/s; a different true speed misplaces reflectors in depth.

connectionEdges.title: Range Ambiguity
connectionEdges.link: When an echo from an earlier pulse arrives after the next pulse, the range equation places it too shallow.

connectionEdges.title: Reverberation, Comet Tail & Ring-Down
connectionEdges.link: Multiple reflections take extra time, so the range equation draws the repeats deeper and evenly spaced.

topics.registryApplication: Expect direct time-to-depth calculations, round-trip traps, and questions predicting where a reflector is displayed when the true speed differs from 1540 m/s.

checkpoint.pearl: 13 µs per cm of depth; 26 µs = 2 cm; slower medium = drawn too deep
checkpoint.reflection: An echo returns 52 µs after the pulse leaves the transducer. How deep is the reflector, and how far did the sound travel in total?

topics.title: Axial Resolution
topics.frontClue: LARRD: longitudinal, axial, range, radial, depth all mean the same thing
topics.corePiece: Axial resolution is the ability to display two structures as separate when they lie one in front of the other, parallel to the beam. Its synonyms form the mnemonic LARRD: longitudinal, axial, range, radial, and depth resolution. Axial resolution (mm) = spatial pulse length / 2; in soft tissue this works out to about 0.77 x number of cycles / frequency in MHz. Smaller numbers mean better resolution. Two reflectors closer together than half the SPL return overlapping echoes and appear as one. Axial resolution improves with shorter pulses: higher frequency (shorter wavelength), fewer cycles per pulse (more damping by the backing material), and wider bandwidth. It is determined by the transducer and the medium, and it does not change with depth because the pulse length stays the same as it travels. The sonographer can improve it only by choosing a higher frequency or a different transducer. In diagnostic imaging, axial resolution is usually better than lateral resolution, because pulses are shorter than beams are wide.
topics.whyLock: The logic is short: short pulse means good axial resolution. Anything that shortens the spatial pulse length helps, and nothing else does. Trap: focusing improves lateral resolution, not axial. Trap two: axial resolution does not vary with depth, but lateral resolution does. Trap three: gain, depth, and PRF have no effect on it. If an answer choice says to increase the number of cycles, that worsens axial resolution. Imaging transducers are heavily damped, with low Q and two or three cycles per pulse, precisely to protect axial resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Pulse Duration & Spatial Pulse Length
connectionEdges.link: Axial resolution is exactly half the spatial pulse length.

connectionEdges.title: Matching Layer & Backing Material
connectionEdges.link: Backing material shortens the pulse by reducing ringing, directly improving axial resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Lateral & Elevational Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Axial depends on pulse length, while lateral depends on beam width and changes with depth.

topics.registryApplication: Questions ask you to calculate it (SPL divided by 2), recognize its synonyms (LARRD), and choose which change improves it, with focusing and depth as typical distractors.

checkpoint.pearl: Axial resolution = SPL / 2; shorter pulse, higher frequency, fewer cycles = better
checkpoint.reflection: A 2-cycle pulse at 5 MHz travels through soft tissue. What is the axial resolution, and would two reflectors 0.2 mm apart be resolved?

categories.description: Crystals, construction, beam shape, and arrays

topics.title: Piezoelectric Effect
topics.frontClue: Squeeze the crystal and it makes voltage; shock it with voltage and it rings
topics.corePiece: Piezoelectric materials convert mechanical energy (pressure) into electrical energy, which is how echoes are received, and convert electrical energy into mechanical vibration, the reverse piezoelectric effect, which is how pulses are transmitted. The most common transducer material is lead zirconate titanate (PZT), a man-made ceramic; natural piezoelectric materials include quartz and tourmaline, and modern composite and single-crystal materials offer wider bandwidth. PZT becomes piezoelectric through polarization: it is heated above its Curie temperature, about 300 to 360 degrees Celsius, in a strong electrical field and then cooled. Heating it above the Curie point again, as in autoclaving, depolarizes the crystal and destroys the transducer. In pulsed ultrasound, the operating (resonant) frequency is determined by the crystal's thickness and its propagation speed: frequency = speed of sound in the crystal / (2 x thickness). Thin crystals and fast crystals produce high frequencies, and the crystal is one half of a wavelength thick. In continuous wave ultrasound, the transmitted frequency equals the frequency of the electrical drive voltage.
topics.whyLock: The exam asks what determines frequency in two flavors: pulsed, where crystal thickness and crystal speed decide, and continuous wave, where the electrical frequency decides. Thin means high frequency. Trap: in pulsed mode, the voltage applied to the crystal changes output strength, not frequency. Trap two: never heat sterilize a probe, because exceeding the Curie temperature depolarizes it. Remember that the same crystal both transmits and receives, so damage to it affects sending and listening alike.

connectionEdges.title: Matching Layer & Backing Material
connectionEdges.link: Layers in front of and behind the crystal shape how efficiently and how briefly it rings.

connectionEdges.title: Bandwidth & Quality Factor
connectionEdges.link: How long the crystal rings after excitation determines the pulse's bandwidth and Q factor.

connectionEdges.title: Transducer Arrays & Steering
connectionEdges.link: Arrays are many small piezoelectric elements fired in patterns to steer and focus.

topics.registryApplication: Look for the definition (pressure creates voltage), PZT and its alternatives, Curie temperature and sterilization, and what sets operating frequency in pulsed versus continuous wave transducers.

checkpoint.pearl: Thin crystal + fast crystal = high frequency; crystal thickness = half a wavelength
checkpoint.reflection: Why would heat sterilization ruin a transducer, and which two crystal properties set the frequency of a pulsed transducer?

topics.title: Matching Layer & Backing Material
topics.frontClue: The front layer helps sound escape; the back layer stops the ringing
topics.corePiece: The matching layer sits on the face of the crystal. PZT has an impedance roughly 20 times higher than skin, so without help most of the sound would reflect at the transducer surface. The matching layer has an impedance between that of PZT and skin, stepping the impedance down and improving transmission in both directions. Its thickness is one quarter of a wavelength. Coupling gel acts as a second matching medium by removing air, since a soft tissue and air boundary reflects nearly all sound. Impedance order: PZT greater than matching layer greater than gel greater than skin. The backing (damping) material sits behind the crystal, typically epoxy resin loaded with tungsten. It absorbs the crystal's ringing and shortens each pulse to about two or three cycles. That reduces pulse duration and spatial pulse length, improves axial resolution, widens bandwidth, lowers the quality factor, and reduces sensitivity. Continuous wave Doppler and therapeutic transducers use little or no backing.
topics.whyLock: Know what each layer changes. The matching layer improves transmission and sensitivity through impedance stepping and is a quarter wavelength thick. The backing makes everything about the pulse shorter and the bandwidth wider, at the cost of sensitivity. Trap: the crystal is half a wavelength thick, while the matching layer is one quarter. Trap two: damping broadens the range of frequencies around the main frequency rather than shifting the main frequency itself. Imaging probes trade a little sensitivity for detail.

connectionEdges.title: Reflection, Impedance & Refraction
connectionEdges.link: The matching layer works by reducing the impedance mismatch that would otherwise reflect sound at the skin.

connectionEdges.title: Axial Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Backing material shortens the pulse, which directly improves axial resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Bandwidth & Quality Factor
connectionEdges.link: Damping widens bandwidth and lowers the quality factor of imaging transducers.

topics.registryApplication: Questions test impedance ordering, the quarter-wavelength rule, the effects of damping (shorter pulse, wider bandwidth, lower Q, less sensitivity), and which transducers lack backing.

checkpoint.pearl: Matching layer = quarter wave, better transmission; backing = fewer cycles, better axial, lower Q
checkpoint.reflection: If a manufacturer removed the backing material, what would happen to pulse length, bandwidth, Q factor, sensitivity, and axial resolution?

topics.title: Bandwidth & Quality Factor
topics.frontClue: A muffled bell gives a short thud with many tones: wide bandwidth, low Q
topics.corePiece: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies contained in a pulse, the difference between its highest and lowest frequencies. A pulse is never a single pure frequency; the shorter the pulse, the more frequencies it contains. Quality factor (Q factor) = main (resonant) frequency / bandwidth, and it has no units. For example, a 6 MHz transducer emitting 4 to 8 MHz has a 4 MHz bandwidth and a Q of 1.5. Fractional bandwidth is the inverse: bandwidth / main frequency. Imaging transducers are heavily damped, so they produce short pulses, wide bandwidth, and a low Q, which supports good axial resolution. Therapeutic and continuous wave Doppler transducers have little or no damping, long or continuous emission, narrow bandwidth, and a high Q. Wide bandwidth is what makes modern techniques possible: multi-frequency probes that let the sonographer select different frequencies, frequency compounding, and harmonic imaging, which transmits at a fundamental frequency and receives at twice that frequency. Pulsed Doppler uses longer pulses and narrower bandwidth than gray-scale imaging.
topics.whyLock: Think of a bell. A well-made bell rings for a long time at one pure tone, which is high Q. Wrap it in cloth and it gives a short thud with many mixed tones, which is low Q. Damping, short pulses, wide bandwidth, low Q, and good axial resolution always travel together. Trap: Q has no units. Trap two: wide bandwidth does not mean a higher center frequency. Doppler favors narrow bandwidth so the frequency shift can be measured precisely.

connectionEdges.link: Backing material is what shortens the pulse and widens the bandwidth.

connectionEdges.link: Harmonic imaging needs bandwidth wide enough to contain both the fundamental and twice the fundamental.

connectionEdges.title: Pulse Duration & Spatial Pulse Length
connectionEdges.link: Pulse duration and bandwidth are inversely related: short pulses contain many frequencies.

topics.title: Beam Anatomy & Focusing
topics.frontClue: Near zone, focus, far zone: the beam pinches to half its width, then spreads
topics.corePiece: An unfocused disc-shaped crystal produces a beam with three regions. The near zone (Fresnel zone) starts at the transducer face, where beam width equals the crystal diameter, and narrows with depth. The focus is the narrowest point, where beam width is one half the crystal diameter; the distance from the face to the focus is the near zone length or focal depth. Beyond the focus, the far zone (Fraunhofer zone) diverges, and at two near zone lengths the beam is again as wide as the crystal. Near zone length = diameter squared x frequency / 6 in soft tissue (diameter in mm, frequency in MHz, length in mm), so a larger diameter and a higher frequency give a deeper focus. Far zone divergence is reduced by the same two factors. Focusing, with a lens, a curved crystal, or electronic phasing, narrows the beam in the focal region and moves the focus shallower, improving lateral resolution near the focus at the cost of greater divergence beyond it.
topics.whyLock: Diameter and frequency both lengthen the near zone and reduce divergence, but frequency is the clean winner because it does so without widening the beam. Trap: a small-diameter crystal has a shallow focus and diverges quickly. Trap two: focusing concentrates energy, so intensity at the focus rises even though power does not. On array transducers, electronic focusing is adjustable: place the focal zone at or just below the structure of interest. Multiple focal zones improve lateral resolution over depth but reduce frame rate.

connectionEdges.title: Lateral & Elevational Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Lateral resolution equals beam width, so it is best at the focus.

connectionEdges.title: Transducer Arrays & Steering
connectionEdges.link: Arrays focus electronically by firing outer elements first and center elements last.

connectionEdges.title: Temporal Resolution & Frame Rate
connectionEdges.link: Each added focal zone requires extra pulses per scan line and lowers frame rate.

topics.registryApplication: Questions ask for beam width at the focus (half the diameter) and at two near zone lengths, which factors deepen the focus, and how focusing changes beam width, intensity, and frame rate.

checkpoint.pearl: Bigger crystal or higher frequency = deeper focus and less divergence
checkpoint.reflection: Two unfocused 6 mm crystals operate at 3 MHz and 6 MHz. Which has the deeper focus, and which beam spreads less in the far zone?

topics.title: Lateral & Elevational Resolution
topics.frontClue: LATA: lateral, angular, transverse, azimuthal, all decided by beam width
topics.corePiece: Lateral resolution is the ability to display two structures as separate when they lie side by side, perpendicular to the beam. Its synonyms form the mnemonic LATA: lateral, angular, transverse, and azimuthal resolution. Lateral resolution (mm) is approximately equal to the beam width at that depth. Because beam width changes with depth, lateral resolution varies with depth: it is best at the focus, where the beam is narrowest, and worse in the near and far zones. It improves with focusing, with correct focal zone placement, and with higher frequency, which reduces far-zone divergence. Line density also contributes: more scan lines per frame sample the field more finely but lower frame rate. Elevational resolution is resolution in the third dimension, perpendicular to the image plane, and it is determined by the slice thickness of the beam. Conventional one-dimensional arrays have a fixed elevational focus set by a lens; 1.5D and 2D arrays focus electronically in elevation and reduce slice thickness artifact.
topics.whyLock: The simplest summary is that lateral resolution comes down to beam width, while axial resolution comes down to pulse length. If a question asks how to improve lateral resolution, look for focusing or moving the focal zone; higher frequency also helps by reducing divergence. Trap: damping and fewer cycles improve axial, not lateral, resolution. Trap two: unlike axial resolution, lateral resolution changes with depth. Poor elevational resolution causes slice thickness artifact, in which echoes from beside the image plane fill in cysts and vessels.

connectionEdges.title: Beam Anatomy & Focusing
connectionEdges.link: Beam width at each depth, set by focusing and crystal size, defines lateral resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Axial Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Axial depends on pulse length and stays constant with depth, while lateral depends on beam width.

connectionEdges.title: Side Lobe, Grating Lobe & Slice Thickness
connectionEdges.link: Poor elevational resolution produces slice thickness artifact that fills in anechoic structures.

topics.registryApplication: Expect synonyms (LATA), where lateral resolution is best (at the focus), which control improves it (focal zone), and what determines elevational resolution (slice thickness).

checkpoint.pearl: Axial = pulse length; lateral = beam width; elevational = slice thickness
checkpoint.reflection: Two side-by-side reflectors 2 mm apart sit where the beam is 3 mm wide. How will they appear, and which control could separate them?

topics.title: Transducer Arrays & Steering
topics.frontClue: Sequential arrays slide the beam; phased arrays steer it with tiny time delays
topics.corePiece: An array is a group of small piezoelectric elements, each with its own wire, fired in patterns. A linear sequential array fires small groups of elements one after another along a flat face, producing a rectangular image. A curvilinear (convex) array uses the same sequencing on a curved face, producing a blunted sector image. A phased array fires all of its elements with tiny time delays to steer and focus the beam electronically, producing a sector image. A vector (linear phased) array combines sequencing with phasing and produces a trapezoidal image. An annular array uses concentric rings that are focused electronically at many depths in both the lateral and elevational planes, but it is steered mechanically. In electronic focusing, outer elements fire first and center elements last, in a curved pattern; in electronic steering, the delays form a sloped pattern. A dead element in a linear sequential array creates a vertical dropout line from top to bottom; in a phased array, it degrades steering and focusing across the whole image.
topics.whyLock: The exam distinguishes arrays by image shape and by what happens when an element fails. Rectangle means linear, blunted sector means curvilinear, a sector with a narrow top means phased, and a trapezoid means vector. The annular array is the odd one: electronic focusing, mechanical steering. Curved delay patterns focus, sloped delay patterns steer, and a curved and sloped pattern does both. Trap: a damaged linear sequential element causes a sharp vertical line of dropout, not general blurring. The regular spacing of elements also creates grating lobes, which manufacturers reduce with subdicing and apodization.

connectionEdges.title: Beam Anatomy & Focusing
connectionEdges.link: Electronic focusing uses curved firing delays to move the focus to the depth the sonographer selects.

connectionEdges.title: Side Lobe, Grating Lobe & Slice Thickness
connectionEdges.link: The regular spacing of array elements produces grating lobes and their artifacts.

connectionEdges.title: Piezoelectric Effect
connectionEdges.link: Each array element is a small piezoelectric crystal that transmits and receives independently.

topics.registryApplication: Questions match array type to image shape, ask how each array steers and focuses, and ask what image results from a damaged element.

topics.title: Receiver Functions
topics.frontClue: A Cold Dog Can Run: amplify, compensate, compress, demodulate, reject
topics.corePiece: The receiver processes returning echoes in a fixed order, remembered as A Cold Dog Can Run: Amplification, Compensation, Compression, Demodulation, Rejection. Amplification, or receiver gain, boosts all signals equally, typically by 60 to 100 dB, and is adjustable. Compensation, or time gain compensation (TGC), boosts deep echoes more than shallow ones to correct for attenuation, so similar tissues look equally bright at every depth; it is adjusted with slide controls. Compression reduces the range of signal strengths, the dynamic range, to fit what the electronics, display, and eye can handle, while preserving the order of bright to dim; it is adjustable. Demodulation converts the signal into a form suitable for display through rectification, which turns negative voltages positive, and smoothing, which traces the envelope; it is the one function the sonographer cannot adjust. Rejection, also called threshold or suppression, eliminates low-level noise and is adjustable. Before reception, the pulser and beam former create and time the transmitted pulses.
topics.whyLock: Order and adjustability are the two features most often tested. Demodulation is the only receiver function the sonographer cannot change. TGC exists only because of attenuation; a TGC curve that is too steep makes the deep field too bright. Trap: gain and TGC change brightness without changing the transmitted energy, so they do not increase patient exposure. Rejection affects only weak signals and leaves bright echoes alone. If the whole image is too dark, adjust overall gain; if it is dark only at depth, adjust TGC.

connectionEdges.title: Output Power vs Receiver Gain
connectionEdges.link: Receiver gain is amplification after the echo returns, unlike output power, which acts on transmission.

connectionEdges.title: Attenuation
connectionEdges.link: Compensation exists solely to correct for attenuation that increases with depth.

connectionEdges.title: Dynamic Range & Compression
connectionEdges.link: Compression is the receiver step that sets the displayed dynamic range.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on the order of the five functions, the one function that is not adjustable (demodulation), and choosing gain versus TGC to correct brightness in one region of an image.

checkpoint.pearl: ACCDR: amplify, compensate, compress, demodulate, reject; demodulation is not adjustable
checkpoint.reflection: The near field looks fine but the image darkens progressively below 8 cm. Which receiver function do you adjust, and why?

topics.title: Output Power vs Receiver Gain
topics.frontClue: Gain brightens the picture; output power brightens the picture and the patient's dose
topics.corePiece: Both controls make the image brighter, but they work at opposite ends of the system. Output power, also called transmit power, acoustic power, or energy output, changes the voltage the pulser applies to the crystals. That increases the amplitude, power, and intensity of the transmitted pulse, strengthens every returning echo, and improves the signal-to-noise ratio, but it also increases patient exposure, including the thermal index and mechanical index. Receiver gain amplifies the echoes after they return to the transducer. It brightens signal and noise equally, so the signal-to-noise ratio does not improve, but patient exposure is unchanged. Following ALARA, when an image is too dark the sonographer should first increase receiver gain, and raise output power only when gain cannot produce a diagnostic image, for example when weak echoes are buried in noise. When an image is too bright, the first step is to reduce output power, which lowers exposure. Output power is the primary control that directly changes the acoustic exposure to the patient.
topics.whyLock: Think about where each control acts: output power before the sound enters the patient, gain after the echoes come back. That one idea explains both the bioeffect and the noise behavior. Trap: increasing gain to improve the signal-to-noise ratio is wrong, because gain amplifies noise too. Trap two: when the image is too bright, the ALARA answer is to decrease output power; when it is too dark, the ALARA answer is to increase gain. Questions often present both options and expect you to pick based on brightness direction.

connectionEdges.title: Receiver Functions
connectionEdges.link: Receiver gain is the first receiver function, amplification, applied to returning echoes.

connectionEdges.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
connectionEdges.link: ALARA dictates using gain before output power because only output power raises exposure.

connectionEdges.title: Amplitude, Power & Intensity
connectionEdges.link: Output power changes transmitted amplitude, power, and intensity together.

topics.registryApplication: Scenario questions ask for the ALARA-correct adjustment to a dark or bright image and which control improves the signal-to-noise ratio (output power, not gain).

checkpoint.pearl: Too dark: gain first. Too bright: power down first. Only output power improves SNR
checkpoint.reflection: A weak echo is lost in background noise. Will turning up receiver gain reveal it, and what change would?

topics.title: Temporal Resolution & Frame Rate
topics.frontClue: Shallow, narrow, one focus, fewer lines: the frames fly
topics.corePiece: Temporal resolution is the ability to accurately position moving structures from instant to instant, and it is determined by frame rate, measured in frames per second (Hz). Higher frame rate means better temporal resolution; frame time is the reciprocal of frame rate. Frame rate is limited by the speed of sound in tissue and by how many pulses each frame requires: frame time = PRP x number of scan lines x number of focal zones, when each focal zone needs its own pulse per line. The sonographer improves frame rate by decreasing imaging depth, which shortens PRP, using a single focal zone, narrowing the sector or image width, and lowering line density. Increasing depth, adding focal zones, widening the sector, or raising line density all lower frame rate. Color Doppler lowers frame rate sharply because each color line requires several pulses, the packet or ensemble, so a small color box helps. Transducer frequency does not change frame rate. Improving spatial resolution with more lines or focal zones costs temporal resolution.
topics.whyLock: Every frame rate question reduces to one idea: how much time does each frame take? Deeper imaging means longer listening for every line, and more focal zones or more lines mean more pulses per frame. Trap: frequency and gain do not affect frame rate. Trap two: persistence smooths the image by averaging frames, which makes moving structures blur and degrades temporal resolution even though frame rate itself is unchanged. For fast-moving structures such as heart valves, reduce depth, sector width, and focal zones first.

connectionEdges.title: PRF & PRP
connectionEdges.link: Each scan line takes at least one PRP, and PRP grows with depth.

connectionEdges.title: Beam Anatomy & Focusing
connectionEdges.link: Every additional focal zone requires extra pulses, trading frame rate for lateral resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Color Doppler
connectionEdges.link: Color packets add many pulses per line, so color boxes are a major cause of low frame rate.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on which change increases frame rate (shallower depth, single focus, narrower sector, lower line density) and on the trade-off between temporal and spatial resolution.

checkpoint.pearl: Depth, focal zones, sector width, or line density up = frame rate down
checkpoint.reflection: You add two focal zones and widen the sector on an echocardiogram. What happens to temporal resolution, and what could you change to recover it?

topics.title: Dynamic Range & Compression
topics.frontClue: Compression squeezes a huge range of echo strengths into usable shades of gray
topics.corePiece: Dynamic range is the ratio of the largest to the smallest signal a system component can handle, expressed in decibels. Echoes returning from the body span an enormous range, far wider than a display or the human eye can show. Compression, the third receiver function, reduces the dynamic range of the signals while preserving their order from strongest to weakest, so they fit the electronics, the display, and the viewer. The sonographer adjusts this with the dynamic range or compression control. Decreasing dynamic range, which means more compression, produces a higher-contrast image with fewer shades of gray: more black and white, with bold edges. Increasing dynamic range, meaning less compression, produces a smoother, lower-contrast image with more gray shades that shows subtle tissue differences. Contrast resolution, the ability to separate echoes of slightly different strength, depends on the number of bits per pixel: n bits give 2 to the power n shades of gray, so 8 bits give 256. Compression has no effect on the sound transmitted into the patient.
topics.whyLock: The vocabulary runs opposite to intuition. More compression means less dynamic range, which means more contrast. Students reverse this often, so say it to yourself in one breath. Use a wide dynamic range for subtle parenchymal texture, such as liver, and a narrower range when you want bold separation, such as fluid against tissue. Trap: compression keeps weak echoes but squeezes them together, while rejection simply discards them. Bits per pixel govern contrast resolution, not spatial resolution.

connectionEdges.title: Receiver Functions
connectionEdges.link: Compression is the third of the five receiver functions.

connectionEdges.title: Preprocessing vs Postprocessing
connectionEdges.link: Gray-scale and contrast adjustments can be applied before or after image storage, which defines how reversible they are.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on which image results from changing dynamic range (high contrast versus smooth gray) and calculations of gray shades from bits per pixel (2 to the n).

checkpoint.pearl: Less dynamic range = more compression = more contrast = fewer grays
checkpoint.reflection: An image looks flat and gray with poorly defined borders. Should you increase or decrease the dynamic range, and what happens to the number of gray shades?

topics.title: Preprocessing vs Postprocessing
topics.frontClue: Before storage it is baked in; after storage you can still tweak a frozen image
topics.corePiece: Image processing is classified by where it occurs relative to image memory in the scan converter. Preprocessing happens before the image is stored: it shapes data as it is acquired, can be applied only to a live image, and cannot be undone or changed on a frozen image. Examples include TGC, write magnification, persistence (frame averaging), spatial compounding, edge enhancement, and fill-in interpolation, which fills gaps between scan lines. Postprocessing happens after storage and can be applied to a frozen image. Examples include read magnification (zoom on stored data), black-and-white inversion, contrast variation, gray-scale maps, 3D rendering, and measurements. Write magnification rescans only the region of interest, assigning more pixels and often more scan lines to it, so spatial resolution genuinely improves. Read magnification simply enlarges stored pixels, so the image gets bigger but no new detail appears. Digital images are built from pixels, and higher pixel density gives better spatial detail. An analog-to-digital converter changes echo signals into binary numbers for storage.
topics.whyLock: The quick test is simple: can it be done to a frozen image? If yes, it is postprocessing. The classic paired question is write versus read magnification. Write magnification acquires new data and improves spatial resolution; read magnification only enlarges existing pixels and can look blocky. Trap: persistence feels like a display effect, but it is preprocessing, and it degrades temporal resolution. Another trap is assuming anything labeled zoom improves detail; only write zoom does.

connectionEdges.link: Gray-scale mapping and contrast changes illustrate how display processing can follow storage.

connectionEdges.link: TGC, a receiver function, is a classic example of preprocessing.

topics.title: Harmonic Imaging & Contrast Agents
topics.frontClue: Transmit at f, listen at 2f: harmonics grow inside the body, not at the skin
topics.corePiece: Tissue harmonic imaging transmits at a fundamental frequency and receives at twice that frequency, the second harmonic. Harmonics are created as the beam travels, through nonlinear propagation: sound travels slightly faster in compressions than in rarefactions, gradually distorting the wave. Harmonics are nearly absent at the skin, build up with depth, and are produced mainly in the strongest central part of the beam. As a result they bypass the superficial layers that cause reverberation and clutter and largely avoid the weak side lobes and grating lobes. The benefits are fewer artifacts, better lateral resolution, and better contrast,. Harmonics can be separated by filtering, which requires a wide bandwidth transducer, or by pulse inversion, which sends two inverted pulses down each line so the fundamental signals cancel and the harmonics remain, at the cost of frame rate. Contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles with a stabilizing shell, roughly the size of or smaller than red blood cells, so they cross capillaries. They reflect strongly and resonate, producing contrast harmonics.
topics.whyLock: The key idea is that tissue harmonics are made in the body, not by the transducer, and they are strongest where the beam is strongest. That single fact explains every benefit. Trap: harmonic imaging does not transmit at 2f; it transmits at f and receives at 2f, which is why penetration is better than simply transmitting the higher frequency. Trap two: contrast harmonics come from microbubble oscillation, not from tissue propagation. Keep the mechanical index low during contrast studies so bubbles oscillate rather than burst, unless destruction is intended.

connectionEdges.link: A wide bandwidth transducer is needed to transmit the fundamental and receive the harmonic.

connectionEdges.link: Mechanical index determines whether contrast microbubbles oscillate or rupture.

connectionEdges.title: Side Lobe, Grating Lobe & Slice Thickness

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on how tissue harmonics form (nonlinear propagation), their benefits (fewer artifacts and better lateral resolution), how pulse inversion works, and the role of mechanical index with microbubbles.

checkpoint.reflection: Why does tissue harmonic imaging reduce reverberation from the abdominal wall, and why does pulse inversion lower frame rate?

topics.title: Advanced Imaging Modes
topics.frontClue: Average many looks to cut noise, but every extra look costs time
topics.corePiece: Spatial compounding steers the beam electronically to several angles and averages the resulting frames into one image. It reduces speckle and noise and sharpens curved or angled boundaries, but it lowers frame rate, can blur motion, and reduces shadowing and enhancement, artifacts that sometimes confirm a diagnosis. Frequency compounding divides a wide bandwidth into sub-bands, forms an image from each, and averages them to reduce speckle. Coded excitation transmits long, encoded pulses and decodes the echoes on reception, improving penetration and signal-to-noise ratio while preserving axial resolution. Extended field of view, or panoramic imaging, stitches frames together as the probe slides along the skin. 3D imaging acquires a volume of data that can be resliced in any plane or rendered; 4D adds real-time motion. Elastography assesses tissue stiffness: strain elastography measures how much tissue deforms under compression, while shear wave elastography measures shear wave speed, which is faster in stiffer tissue. M-mode displays depth versus time along a single scan line and has the best temporal resolution of any mode.
topics.whyLock: Most advanced modes trade time for image quality: averaging several acquisitions improves the picture but lowers frame rate. Trap: spatial compounding reduces the shadowing and enhancement that help identify stones and cysts, so turn it off when you need those clues. Shear wave speed increases with stiffness, and the shear wave is a separate, much slower wave than the imaging pulse. M-mode samples one line thousands of times per second, so it wins any question about temporal resolution.

topics.title: Reverberation, Comet Tail & Ring-Down
topics.frontClue: Sound trapped between two mirrors builds a ladder of fake echoes going deeper
topics.corePiece: Reverberation occurs when sound bounces back and forth between two strong parallel reflectors, or between a strong reflector and the transducer face. Each extra round trip adds travel time, and because the range equation assumes every echo made exactly one trip, the system plots multiple equally spaced, progressively weaker echoes deeper than the true reflector and parallel to it. The spacing equals the distance between the two reflectors. Comet tail is a form of reverberation in which the two reflectors are so close together (surgical clips, cholesterol crystals in adenomyomatosis, the pleural line) that the echoes merge into a short, tapering, solid bright tail. Ring-down looks similar but has a different mechanism: fluid trapped among a cluster of gas bubbles resonates and emits sound continuously, producing a long, unbroken bright streak that runs toward the bottom of the image. Ring-down signals gas; comet tail signals a small, strong reflector. All three line up along the scan line, deep to the real reflector.
topics.whyLock: Reason from the range equation: the machine converts time to depth at 13 microseconds per centimeter and assumes a single bounce. Extra bounces mean extra time, so the false echoes always land deeper, never shallower. Equal spacing is the giveaway for classic reverberation; a solid, continuous streak points to comet tail or ring-down. A common trap is treating comet tail and ring-down as the same thing: comet tail is reverberation between closely spaced reflectors, while ring-down is resonance of fluid trapped between gas bubbles. Changing the transducer angle or acoustic window and using harmonic imaging reduce reverberation; turning down overall gain only makes the real echoes dimmer too.

connectionEdges.title: Range Equation
connectionEdges.link: Reverberation exists because the range equation assumes one round trip, so each extra bounce is plotted deeper by 13 microseconds per centimeter.

topics.title: Mirror Image
topics.frontClue: A strong reflector acts like a mirror, and the copy always hides deeper
topics.corePiece: Mirror image artifact appears when a strong, smooth specular reflector, classically the diaphragm-lung interface, the pleura, or a bowel-gas interface, redirects the beam toward a real structure and the echo returns along the same detour. The system assumes straight-line travel and a single reflection, so it places a second copy of the structure on the far side of the reflector. The rules to memorize: the true object is closer to the transducer; the copy is deeper; the reflector lies on a straight line between them; and the copy sits as far behind the reflector as the real object sits in front of it. The duplicate may be slightly weaker. Mirror image occurs in grayscale, color Doppler (a duplicate subclavian artery deep to the pleura), and spectral Doppler. The classic example is liver tissue displayed above the diaphragm, where aerated lung should look dark. The spectral mirror from cross talk is a different artifact with a different cause.
topics.whyLock: Mirror image breaks the straight-line path assumption and adds travel time, which is why the copy always lands deeper. Do not confuse it with refraction, which places copies side by side at the same depth, or with reverberation, which produces multiple equally spaced copies. A big trap is the spectral mirror (cross talk): a copy of the waveform across the baseline caused by a beam-to-flow angle near 90 degrees and excessive Doppler gain, not by a specular reflector. True mirror image changes or disappears when you change the scanning window or angle. Clinically, mirrored liver above the diaphragm is reassuring: a pleural effusion removes the reflective lung interface, so the mirror vanishes.

connectionEdges.title: Refraction & Propagation Speed Error
connectionEdges.link: Refraction duplicates a structure side by side at the same depth, whereas mirror image duplicates it deeper, behind the reflector.

connectionEdges.title: Reverberation, Comet Tail & Ring-Down
connectionEdges.link: Both arise from strong specular reflectors and extra travel time, but reverberation yields many equally spaced copies instead of one.

connectionEdges.title: Color & Spectral Doppler Artifacts
connectionEdges.link: The spectral mirror (cross talk) shares the name but comes from a near 90 degree angle and high gain, not a reflector.

checkpoint.pearl: Real object shallow, copy deep, strong reflector in between at equal distances.

topics.title: Shadowing & Enhancement
topics.frontClue: Too much attenuation casts a shadow; too little leaves a bright trail
topics.corePiece: Shadowing and enhancement are attenuation artifacts. They exist because TGC compensates for the average attenuation of soft tissue (about 0.5 dB/cm/MHz). Acoustic shadowing is a hypoechoic or anechoic band deep to a structure that attenuates more than soft tissue, by strong reflection, absorption, or both: gallstones, renal stones, bone, calcified plaque, and gas. The shadow is clean behind stones and bone and dirty (filled with reverberation) behind gas. Posterior acoustic enhancement is the opposite: a hyperechoic band deep to a structure that attenuates less than surrounding tissue, such as a cyst, the gallbladder, the urinary bladder, or ascites, so TGC over-amplifies the echoes behind it. Edge shadowing is a thin shadow at the curved edges of a round structure, caused by refraction and beam divergence rather than attenuation. Focal enhancement (focal banding) is a horizontal bright band at the focal depth, where intensity is highest. Shadowing and enhancement appear deep to the structure, along the beam path.
topics.whyLock: These artifacts help diagnosis: shadowing supports a stone or calcification, and enhancement supports fluid. The trap is thinking enhancement makes the structure itself bright; the structure is anechoic, and it is the tissue behind it that brightens because less energy was lost on the way. Keep the direction straight: high attenuation produces a shadow, low attenuation produces enhancement. Spatial compounding averages beams from several angles and can fill in shadows, so turning it off can reveal a subtle stone shadow. Small stones shadow best when placed in the focal zone and scanned with a higher frequency. Edge shadows form at curved surfaces, not behind stones, so they do not imply calcification.

connectionEdges.title: Attenuation
connectionEdges.link: Shadowing and enhancement are visible evidence of a structure attenuating more or less than the soft tissue average.

connectionEdges.title: Receiver Functions
connectionEdges.link: TGC compensates for average attenuation, so it over-amplifies echoes behind fluid and cannot recover echoes behind a stone.

connectionEdges.title: Refraction & Propagation Speed Error
connectionEdges.link: Edge shadows at the margins of round structures are caused by refraction, not by attenuation.

topics.registryApplication: Expect images of gallstones with shadowing or a cyst with enhancement and questions on the cause (high versus low attenuation) or on edge shadow from refraction.

checkpoint.pearl: Shadow = more attenuation than tissue; enhancement = less attenuation than tissue.
checkpoint.reflection: Why does a fluid-filled cyst make the tissue behind it look brighter if the cyst itself reflects almost nothing?
