topics.title: Side Lobe, Grating Lobe & Slice Thickness
topics.frontClue: Off-axis energy and a thick beam drop phantom echoes into empty spaces
topics.corePiece: These are beam-width artifacts: the system assumes every echo came from a thin main beam along its central axis. Side lobes are weak off-axis beams produced by single-element and array transducers; grating lobes are additional off-axis beams in array transducers, caused by the regular spacing of the elements. When a lobe strikes a strong reflector, the echo is displayed as if it came from the main beam, placing false low-level echoes inside anechoic structures such as the gallbladder, bladder, or a cyst, often mimicking sludge, or placing a copy of a bright structure beside the real one. Grating lobes are reduced by subdicing (cutting elements into smaller pieces) and apodization; side lobes are reduced by apodization and harmonic imaging. Slice thickness (elevational resolution) artifact arises because the beam has finite thickness perpendicular to the image plane, so echoes from tissue just above or below the plane fill in anechoic structures. It is reduced by elevational focusing (a lens or 1.5-D and 2-D arrays) and harmonics, not by TGC.
topics.whyLock: Ask where the extra echo came from. A false echo beside a bright reflector points to side or grating lobes; low-level fill-in of a cyst or bladder suggests slice thickness. The classic trap is pseudo-sludge: before calling debris, reposition the patient, because real sludge layers dependently and moves while artifactual echoes do not follow gravity. Another trap is choosing lower gain or TGC as the fix; that only hides echoes and does not narrow the beam. Harmonic imaging helps both side lobes and slice thickness because harmonic energy is generated mainly in the strong central beam. Slice thickness is elevational resolution, and it is best at the elevational focus.

connectionEdges.title: Lateral & Elevational Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Slice thickness artifact is a failure of elevational resolution, and lobes degrade lateral image accuracy.

connectionEdges.title: Transducer Arrays & Steering
connectionEdges.link: Grating lobes are a product of evenly spaced array elements and are reduced by subdicing and apodization.

connectionEdges.title: Harmonic Imaging & Contrast Agents
connectionEdges.link: Harmonic signals form mainly in the strong central beam, so harmonics suppress side lobe and slice thickness echoes.

topics.registryApplication: Usually shown as false echoes in the gallbladder or bladder; questions ask for the artifact name or the correct fix (harmonics, elevational focusing, subdicing, apodization) with gain or TGC as distractors.

checkpoint.pearl: Lobes misplace strong echoes sideways; slice thickness fills empty spaces; neither is fixed by gain.
checkpoint.reflection: Echoes fill the edge of a bladder and do not move when the patient rolls. Which artifact is likely and what reduces it?

images.caption: Side lobe artifact: false echoes inside the anechoic gallbladder
Slice thickness artifact: low-level echoes filling part of the urinary bladder

topics.title: Refraction & Propagation Speed Error
topics.frontClue: Bent beam means a sideways error; wrong speed means a depth error
topics.corePiece: Both artifacts break an assumption: sound travels in a straight line at 1540 m/s. Refraction is bending of the transmitted beam at an interface, and it requires two conditions: oblique incidence and different propagation speeds on either side. Snell's law describes it: sine of the transmission angle divided by sine of the incident angle equals speed 2 divided by speed 1. Because the system places every echo along the straight scan line, refracted echoes are displaced laterally, so a structure appears in the wrong side-to-side position or duplicated side by side at the same depth. The classic example is deep to the rectus abdominis muscles, where one aorta, SMA, or gestational sac can appear doubled. Propagation speed error is a depth error. The system uses 1540 m/s in the range equation, so if the true medium is slower (fat is about 1450 m/s), echoes return late and are displayed too deep; if faster, too shallow. The result is a step-off in a straight structure such as the diaphragm.
topics.whyLock: Sort artifacts by the direction of error. Duplication side by side at the same depth means refraction; extra copies deeper means mirror image or reverberation; a structure in the right lateral position but at the wrong depth means propagation speed error. Keep the direction straight: slower medium, longer return time, displayed too deep. A trap is thinking refraction can occur with normal incidence; no matter how different the speeds, a perpendicular beam is not bent. Another trap: an impedance difference determines reflection, while a speed difference determines refraction. Fix refraction by changing the transducer angle or window, for example scanning slightly off midline to avoid the rectus muscles.

connectionEdges.title: Reflection, Impedance & Refraction
connectionEdges.link: Snell's law and the two requirements for refraction, oblique incidence and a speed change, are the physics behind this artifact.

connectionEdges.title: Propagation Speed
connectionEdges.link: The machine assumes 1540 m/s, so tissues slower or faster than that produce depth errors.

connectionEdges.title: Range Equation
connectionEdges.link: Propagation speed error is the range equation applied with the wrong speed, misplacing echoes in depth.

topics.registryApplication: Expect a duplicated aorta or gestational sac deep to the rectus muscles (refraction) or a question asking where a structure is displayed when the medium is slower than 1540 m/s (too deep).

checkpoint.pearl: Refraction errs sideways; speed error errs in depth; slow medium means too deep.
checkpoint.reflection: A reflector lies behind a fatty mass with a speed of 1450 m/s. Is it displayed too shallow or too deep, and why?

images.caption: Refraction artifact: one deep structure displayed twice, side by side at the same depth

topics.title: Range Ambiguity
topics.frontClue: An echo from the last pulse arrives late and gets blamed on the next one
topics.corePiece: Range ambiguity occurs when the PRF is too high for the depth being imaged. The system assumes each echo belongs to the most recent pulse and assigns depth with the range equation (13 microseconds of round-trip time per centimeter). If a strong reflector lies deeper than the listening time allows, its echo from pulse 1 can arrive after pulse 2 has been sent. The system then times it from pulse 2 and places it far too shallow, often as a faint echo inside a cyst or other anechoic region. To prevent this, the pulse repetition period must be long enough for echoes from the deepest reflector to return before the next pulse: the minimum PRP is 13 microseconds times the depth in centimeters, and the maximum PRF is about 77,000 divided by the depth in centimeters. Increasing the depth setting lowers the PRF automatically and eliminates the artifact. In Doppler, high PRF mode deliberately accepts range ambiguity, with several sample volumes active along the beam, to measure higher velocities.
topics.whyLock: Range ambiguity is distinctive because it places echoes too shallow, while the multipath artifacts (reverberation, mirror image) place them too deep. It ties together PRF, depth, and the Nyquist limit: imaging deeper forces a lower PRF, which reduces frame rate and the Doppler Nyquist limit. High PRF Doppler trades certainty about depth for a higher Nyquist limit. Trap: choosing decrease depth as the fix; that raises the PRF and makes the problem worse. The correct fix is to increase the depth (lower the PRF). A suspicious echo that moves or disappears when the depth or PRF changes is range ambiguity.

connectionEdges.title: PRF & PRP
connectionEdges.link: The artifact appears when the PRP is too short for echoes from deep reflectors to return before the next pulse.

connectionEdges.title: Range Equation
connectionEdges.link: The system times each echo from the latest pulse, so a late echo from an earlier pulse is assigned a falsely shallow depth.

connectionEdges.title: Continuous Wave vs Pulsed Wave
connectionEdges.link: CW Doppler and high PRF Doppler both give up precise depth information in exchange for measuring higher velocities.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as which artifact places echoes too shallow, what causes it (PRF too high for depth), or how to fix it (increase depth, lowering PRF).

checkpoint.pearl: Too many pulses per second means late echoes are placed too shallow; increase depth to fix it.
checkpoint.reflection: Why does increasing the depth setting eliminate range ambiguity?

topics.title: Color & Spectral Doppler Artifacts
topics.frontClue: Wall noise, mirror copies, sparkle behind stones, and color bleeding past the walls
topics.corePiece: Beyond aliasing, several Doppler artifacts appear on the exam. Clutter is low-velocity, high-amplitude signal from moving vessel walls or tissue; it appears as bright bands hugging the baseline in spectral Doppler (wall thump) and as color ghosting spilling into tissue in color Doppler. The wall filter, a high-pass filter, removes it; set too high, it also erases real slow flow. Spectral mirror (cross talk) is a weaker copy of the spectrum on the opposite side of the baseline, caused by a beam-to-flow angle near 90 degrees and excessive Doppler gain; improve the angle and lower the gain. Blooming is color spilling beyond the vessel walls from excessive color gain. Flash artifact is a burst of color from patient, organ, or transducer motion and is most troublesome in power Doppler. Twinkle artifact is a rapidly changing mix of colors behind a rough, strongly reflective surface such as a renal stone, and it helps confirm a calculus.
topics.whyLock: Organize by control. Gain problems (blooming, spectral mirror, color noise in tissue) are fixed by lowering gain. Motion problems (clutter, flash) are fixed with the wall filter, breath-holding, or a steadier probe. Angle problems (spectral mirror, a color gap in a vessel at 90 degrees) are fixed by steering or repositioning. A common misconception is that clutter is only a color Doppler problem; it occurs in both spectral and color Doppler. Another is confusing the spectral mirror with aliasing: aliasing wraps the peaks around the baseline and is fixed with scale or baseline, while mirroring duplicates the entire waveform and is fixed with angle and gain.

connectionEdges.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
connectionEdges.link: Aliasing is the most tested Doppler artifact, and it must be distinguished from the spectral mirror and true flow reversal.

connectionEdges.title: Color Doppler
connectionEdges.link: Blooming, ghosting, and twinkle are color Doppler artifacts controlled by color gain, wall filter, and scale.

connectionEdges.title: Power Doppler
connectionEdges.link: Power Doppler's high sensitivity and slow frame rate make it especially prone to flash artifact.

topics.registryApplication: Expect a tracing or color image with the question asking for the artifact name or the single best fix, such as increase the wall filter for clutter or fix the angle and reduce gain for spectral mirror.

checkpoint.pearl: Clutter: wall filter. Blooming: lower color gain. Spectral mirror: fix the 90 degree angle and lower gain.
checkpoint.reflection: A spectral tracing shows a fainter copy of the waveform below the baseline. What two settings would you change?

images.caption: Spectral mirror (cross talk): a weaker copy of the waveform below the baseline
Twinkle artifact: rapidly changing mosaic color deep to a renal stone

topics.title: Doppler Equation & Angle
topics.frontClue: The shift doubles with frequency or speed, and the cosine taxes every angle
topics.corePiece: The Doppler shift is the difference between the transmitted and received frequency caused by moving reflectors, mainly red blood cells: fD = 2 x f0 x v x cos(theta) / c, where f0 is the transmitted frequency, v the blood velocity, theta the angle between the beam and the direction of flow, and c the propagation speed (1540 m/s). The factor 2 reflects a double shift: the moving cell receives a shifted wave and reflects it while still moving. Shifts usually fall in the audible range. The shift is directly proportional to velocity, transmitted frequency, and cos(theta). Cos 0 degrees = 1 (full shift), cos 60 degrees = 0.5, and cos 90 degrees = 0 (no shift). The system rearranges the equation to report velocity, v = fD x c / (2 x f0 x cos(theta)), using the angle the sonographer sets with angle correction. Flow toward the transducer gives a positive shift. Vascular protocols use an angle of 60 degrees or less.
topics.whyLock: The equation answers every what-happens-if question: double the frequency and the shift doubles; double the velocity and the shift doubles; move from 0 to 60 degrees and the shift halves. The machine reports velocity, not shift, so a misplaced angle-correction cursor gives a wrong velocity even though the measured shift is real. Errors grow at steep angles because cosine changes fastest there: a 5 degree error at 60 degrees produces about a 15 percent velocity error, versus less than 1 percent near 0 degrees. Trap: the transducer frequency changes the shift, not the actual blood velocity. At exactly 90 degrees no shift is detected, even with fast flow.

connectionEdges.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
connectionEdges.link: Anything that raises the Doppler shift, such as higher frequency or a smaller angle, pushes the signal toward the Nyquist limit.

connectionEdges.title: Spectral Analysis
connectionEdges.link: The spectral display plots the shift, converted to velocity with this equation, over time.

connectionEdges.title: Propagation Speed
connectionEdges.link: The equation assumes c = 1540 m/s, the same soft tissue speed used for imaging.

topics.registryApplication: Expect proportionality questions (what happens to the shift if frequency doubles or the angle goes from 0 to 60 degrees) and recognition that 90 degrees produces no shift.

checkpoint.pearl: fD = 2 x f0 x v x cos(theta) / c: shift tracks frequency, velocity, and cosine; zero at 90 degrees.
checkpoint.reflection: If the angle changes from 0 to 60 degrees with all else equal, what happens to the measured Doppler shift?

topics.title: Continuous Wave vs Pulsed Wave
topics.frontClue: CW never stops talking and never aliases, but it cannot tell you where
topics.corePiece: Continuous wave (CW) Doppler uses two crystals: one transmits constantly while the other receives constantly. Because there are no pulses, there is no PRF and therefore no Nyquist limit, so CW measures very high velocities without aliasing. The trade-off is range ambiguity: signals from anywhere in the overlap of the transmit and receive beams are detected together, so CW cannot tell which depth the signal comes from. CW transducers have no backing material, which gives a high Q factor, narrow bandwidth, and high sensitivity; they are used for high-velocity jets such as aortic stenosis. Pulsed wave (PW) Doppler uses one crystal that alternates between sending and listening. Range gating opens the receiver only for a brief interval, placing a sample volume at a chosen depth and giving range resolution. The cost is a velocity ceiling: PRF limits the maximum measurable shift (Nyquist limit = PRF / 2), so high velocities alias, especially at depth. Doppler pulses are longer than imaging pulses, typically 5 to 30 cycles.
topics.whyLock: The exam frames this as a choice of trade-offs. CW gives unlimited velocity measurement but no range resolution; PW gives range resolution but a velocity ceiling. If a question describes aliasing that persists after raising the scale and dropping the baseline, switching to CW is the answer. If it describes needing the exact location of a stenosis, or separating signals from two overlapping vessels, PW is the answer. High PRF Doppler is a hybrid: extra sample volumes raise the Nyquist limit at the cost of some range ambiguity. Trap: CW is said to have range ambiguity, not range resolution, because its sensitive zone cannot be selected along the beam.

connectionEdges.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
connectionEdges.link: PW Doppler is limited by the Nyquist limit of PRF / 2, while CW has no PRF and never aliases.

connectionEdges.title: Range Ambiguity
connectionEdges.link: CW and high PRF Doppler give up depth certainty in exchange for higher measurable velocities.

connectionEdges.title: Bandwidth & Quality Factor
connectionEdges.link: Undamped CW crystals have a narrow bandwidth and high Q, unlike damped pulsed transducers.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as which Doppler mode avoids aliasing (CW), which provides range resolution (PW), or how many crystals each uses.

checkpoint.pearl: CW: two crystals, no aliasing, no depth. PW: one crystal, depth via range gate, aliases above PRF / 2.
checkpoint.reflection: A jet aliases even with the scale at maximum and the baseline at the bottom. What is the next step, and what do you give up?

topics.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
topics.frontClue: Wagon wheels spin backward on film when you sample too slowly
topics.corePiece: Pulsed Doppler samples the returning signal once per pulse, so it can only measure shifts up to the Nyquist limit: Nyquist limit = PRF / 2. When the Doppler shift exceeds this limit, the system cannot determine the true frequency or direction, and the signal wraps around. In spectral Doppler, the tops of the peaks are cut off and appear below the baseline. In color Doppler, the fastest flow wraps directly from the brightest forward color into the brightest reverse color with no black band between them, whereas true flow reversal passes through black. Aliasing is more likely with high velocities, high transducer frequencies (larger shifts), deep sample volumes (more listening time, so lower PRF), and low scale settings. Fixes: raise the scale (PRF), lower the baseline (a display change), use a lower-frequency transducer, choose a shallower window or depth, increase the Doppler angle (smaller shift, though more angle error), or switch to CW Doppler, which never aliases.
topics.whyLock: Think of aliasing as sampling too slowly for how fast the signal changes. Anything that lowers the PRF (a deeper gate) or raises the shift (faster flow, higher frequency, smaller angle) pushes toward aliasing. Example: a PRF of 5 kHz gives a Nyquist limit of 2.5 kHz, so a 3 kHz shift aliases. Trap: moving the baseline does not change the Nyquist limit; it only reassigns the display range so more of it is used in one direction. Another trap is reading color aliasing as flow reversal: true reversal has a black band between the colors. Color aliasing can also help, flagging the high-velocity jet at a stenosis.

connectionEdges.title: PRF & PRP
connectionEdges.link: The Nyquist limit is half the PRF, and a deeper sample volume forces a lower PRF.

connectionEdges.title: Doppler Equation & Angle
connectionEdges.link: Higher transmitted frequency, higher velocity, and smaller angles raise the shift toward the aliasing threshold.

connectionEdges.title: Continuous Wave vs Pulsed Wave
connectionEdges.link: CW Doppler has no PRF and therefore no Nyquist limit, making it the definitive cure for aliasing.

topics.registryApplication: Expect a wrapped spectral tracing or a color image with adjacent bright red and blue, followed by a question on the cause or the best fix (increase scale, lower baseline, lower frequency, use CW).

checkpoint.pearl: Nyquist = PRF / 2; exceed it and the signal wraps. Raise the scale before anything else.
checkpoint.reflection: Which three changes reduce aliasing without changing transducers, and which one only changes the display?

images.caption: Spectral aliasing: systolic peaks wrap around and appear below the baseline
Color aliasing: bright forward colors wrap directly into reverse colors with no black between

topics.title: Spectral Analysis
topics.frontClue: FFT sorts the echo into every speed present at every instant
topics.corePiece: Spectral analysis breaks the complex returning Doppler signal into its individual frequency components. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is the method used for PW and CW Doppler; autocorrelation is used for color Doppler because it is faster but less detailed. On the spectral display, the horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is Doppler shift or velocity, and brightness represents amplitude, which reflects how many red blood cells are moving at that velocity. Laminar flow in a medium or large vessel produces a narrow band of velocities with a clear spectral window beneath the trace. Spectral broadening is filling in of that window, meaning a wide range of velocities. It accompanies turbulence distal to a stenosis, but also a large sample volume, a gate near the wall, or excessive gain. Peak systolic velocity, end-diastolic velocity, resistive index ((PSV - EDV) / PSV), and pulsatility index ((PSV - EDV) / mean velocity) are measured from this display.
topics.whyLock: Read the display axis by axis: horizontal is time, vertical is velocity, brightness is how many cells. A trap: brightness is not velocity; a bright area at low velocity means many slow cells. Spectral broadening is not proof of disease, because an oversized gate or excess gain also produces it, so standardize the sample volume before interpreting. Another trap is mixing up processing methods: FFT for spectral Doppler, autocorrelation for color. Waveform shape reflects downstream resistance: low-resistance beds such as the brain and kidney show continuous diastolic flow, while high-resistance beds such as resting limb muscle show triphasic flow with brief reversal in early diastole.

connectionEdges.title: Doppler Equation & Angle
connectionEdges.link: Each vertical point on the spectrum is a Doppler shift converted to velocity with the Doppler equation.

connectionEdges.title: Laminar vs Turbulent Flow
connectionEdges.link: Laminar flow leaves a clear spectral window; turbulence fills it with spectral broadening.

connectionEdges.title: Color Doppler
connectionEdges.link: Color uses autocorrelation to estimate a mean velocity, while spectral Doppler uses FFT to show the full range.

topics.registryApplication: Typically tested by asking what each axis or brightness represents, which processing method is used (FFT versus autocorrelation), and what causes spectral broadening.

checkpoint.pearl: X = time, Y = velocity, brightness = number of cells; FFT for spectral, autocorrelation for color.
checkpoint.reflection: Name two technical causes of spectral broadening that do not indicate disease.

topics.title: Color Doppler
topics.frontClue: A map of mean velocity: direction by the color bar, not red equals artery
topics.corePiece: Color Doppler is a two-dimensional map of mean Doppler shift (average velocity) and direction, superimposed on the grayscale image. It uses autocorrelation and sends multiple pulses down each scan line, called the packet or ensemble. Colors follow the color bar: the top half shows flow toward the transducer, the bottom half flow away, and black at the baseline means no detected flow or flow below the wall filter. The mnemonic BART (blue away, red toward) describes the usual map, but colors can be inverted, so red does not mean artery. Color Doppler is pulsed, so it has range resolution and aliases above PRF / 2. Because each scan line needs a packet of pulses, color costs temporal resolution: a wider or deeper color box or a larger packet size lowers the frame rate. A larger packet improves slow-flow sensitivity. Color is angle dependent: a straight vessel on a sector image changes color across the field and shows a black gap where the beam is perpendicular.
topics.whyLock: Color reports a mean velocity, not the peak, so it is semi-quantitative; spectral Doppler measures peak velocity. To raise the frame rate, narrow the color box, reduce depth, or reduce packet size, accepting less sensitivity. A black gap where a vessel runs perpendicular to the beam is not thrombus: steer the box or angle the probe. Traps include assuming red always means artery and confusing aliasing (bright red touching bright blue, no black) with true reversal (colors separated by black). Excessive color gain causes blooming, while too little gain, or too high a scale or wall filter, makes slow flow disappear.

connectionEdges.title: Temporal Resolution & Frame Rate
connectionEdges.link: Each color line needs a packet of pulses, so larger color boxes and packets lower the frame rate.

connectionEdges.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
connectionEdges.link: Color is pulsed, so it aliases above PRF / 2, seen as bright forward color touching bright reverse color.

connectionEdges.title: Power Doppler
connectionEdges.link: Power Doppler drops direction and velocity information to gain sensitivity and avoid aliasing.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on what color represents (mean velocity and direction), how box size and packet size affect frame rate, and how to tell aliasing from true flow reversal.

checkpoint.pearl: Color = mean velocity plus direction; bigger box or packet = slower frame rate; black separates true reversal.
checkpoint.reflection: A straight vessel scanned with a sector probe shows red on one side, blue on the other, and black in the middle. Is flow reversing?

images.caption: Excess color gain: color speckles bleed into stationary tissue around the vessel

topics.title: Power Doppler
topics.frontClue: It counts how many cells are moving, not which way or how fast
topics.corePiece: Power Doppler (also called energy or amplitude Doppler) maps the strength, or amplitude, of the Doppler signal, which reflects the number of moving red blood cells, rather than the frequency of the shift. Because it ignores velocity and direction, it gains three key advantages over color Doppler. It is more sensitive to slow and low-volume flow, often quoted as several times more sensitive. It is far less angle dependent, displaying flow at angles near 90 degrees where color drops out. And it does not alias, because the shift frequency is not being measured. Typical uses include suspected testicular or ovarian torsion, low-flow vessels, organ perfusion, and confirming a near-occlusion versus occlusion. The disadvantages mirror its strengths: no direction information in standard power Doppler, no velocity information, lower temporal resolution because heavy averaging slows the frame rate, and high susceptibility to flash artifact from patient, organ, or transducer motion. Some systems offer a directional power mode, but standard power Doppler is non-directional.
topics.whyLock: When a question asks which mode is best for very slow or low-volume flow, the answer is power Doppler. When answer choices list no aliasing or angle independence, consider both power Doppler and CW, and separate them: power Doppler shows no velocity at all, whereas CW measures velocity without depth. Flash is the classic power Doppler artifact; reduce it with breath-holding, a steady probe, or flash suppression. Trap: power Doppler is not truly angle independent at exactly 90 degrees, where there is essentially no shift to detect, but it handles near-perpendicular angles far better than color.

connectionEdges.title: Color Doppler
connectionEdges.link: Both are color-encoded maps, but color shows mean velocity and direction while power shows amplitude only.

connectionEdges.title: Color & Spectral Doppler Artifacts
connectionEdges.link: Flash artifact from tissue or probe motion is the signature power Doppler artifact.

connectionEdges.title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Limit
connectionEdges.link: Because power Doppler does not measure shift frequency, it is not subject to aliasing.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as the best mode for slow flow or torsion, or as a list of advantages (sensitivity, no aliasing, less angle dependence) and disadvantages (no direction or velocity, flash, slow frame rate).

checkpoint.pearl: Power Doppler = amplitude only: most sensitive, no aliasing, no direction, flash-prone.

topics.title: Pressure, Flow & Resistance
topics.frontClue: Flow needs a pressure difference, and halving the radius multiplies resistance by 16
topics.corePiece: Blood moves only when there is a pressure gradient, flowing from high to low pressure. Volumetric flow (Q) is volume per unit time (mL/min), not velocity (cm/s). The relationship is the hydraulic form of Ohm's law: Q = delta P / R. Poiseuille's law describes laminar flow in a long straight tube: Q = delta P x pi x r^4 / (8 x L x viscosity), so resistance R = 8 x L x viscosity / (pi x r^4). Resistance increases in direct proportion to vessel length and blood viscosity and inversely with the fourth power of radius: halving the radius raises resistance 16 times. Radius dominates, which is why arterioles control peripheral resistance. Resistances in series add (R total = R1 + R2 + ...), so the total exceeds any single resistor; in parallel, reciprocals add, so the total is less than any single branch. Volume flow also equals average velocity times area (Q = v x A).
topics.whyLock: Most questions hinge on proportionality. Doubling length doubles resistance; doubling viscosity doubles resistance; halving the radius multiplies resistance by 16, so flow falls to one sixteenth if the pressure gradient stays the same. Do not confuse flow (volume per time) with velocity (speed): in a stenosis, velocity rises while volume flow is maintained until the narrowing becomes severe. Parallel beds lower total resistance, which is why exercise, by opening many muscle beds, lowers distal resistance and turns a triphasic limb waveform into a monophasic one. Remember also that energy drives flow, so pressure, kinetic, and gravitational energy all contribute.

connectionEdges.title: Laminar vs Turbulent Flow
connectionEdges.link: Poiseuille's law applies only to laminar flow; turbulence adds energy loss beyond what it predicts.

connectionEdges.title: Bernoulli & Continuity
connectionEdges.link: Q = v x A is the continuity equation, which explains why velocity rises through a stenosis.

connectionEdges.title: Venous Hemodynamics
connectionEdges.link: Venous return depends on pressure gradients shaped by gravity, respiration, and the muscle pump.

topics.registryApplication: Expect proportionality calculations (effect of halving radius or doubling length or viscosity on resistance or flow) and series versus parallel resistance questions.

checkpoint.pearl: Q = delta P / R; R rises with length and viscosity and falls with radius to the fourth power.
checkpoint.reflection: If vessel radius is halved while the pressure gradient is constant, by what factor does flow change?

topics.title: Laminar vs Turbulent Flow
topics.frontClue: Orderly layers below 1500, chaos above 2000: Reynolds keeps score
topics.corePiece: Laminar flow moves in smooth, parallel layers. In parabolic laminar flow, velocity is highest at the center of the vessel and lowest at the walls because of friction (viscous drag); the average velocity is half the peak center velocity. Plug flow is laminar flow in which all layers travel at nearly the same velocity, typical at the entrance of large vessels such as the proximal aorta; it gives a narrow spectral band with a clear window. Disturbed flow is still laminar but its layers change direction, as at bifurcations and the carotid bulb. Turbulent flow is chaotic and multidirectional, with eddies and vortices, and wastes energy as heat and sound (a bruit, or a palpable thrill). The Reynolds number predicts it: Re = (density x average velocity x diameter) / viscosity. Re below 1500 indicates laminar flow; above 2000, turbulent flow. Turbulence appears just distal to a stenosis, where a high-velocity jet exits into a wider lumen, and is more likely in anemia, where low viscosity raises the Reynolds number.
topics.whyLock: Turbulence is a downstream event: look for it just past a stenosis, in the post-stenotic zone, rather than inside the narrowest segment, where flow is fast but often still organized. On spectral Doppler it produces spectral broadening with simultaneous forward and reverse signals; on color, a mosaic. Raising velocity or diameter, or lowering viscosity, increases the Reynolds number. Trap: plug flow and parabolic flow are both laminar. Another trap: the average velocity of parabolic flow is half the peak, so a volume flow calculation that uses peak velocity overestimates flow. Energy lost to turbulence contributes to the pressure drop across a stenosis.

connectionEdges.link: Laminar flow keeps a clear spectral window; turbulence causes spectral broadening and bidirectional signals.

connectionEdges.title: Bernoulli & Continuity
connectionEdges.link: The velocity jet predicted by continuity at a stenosis becomes turbulent as it expands downstream.

connectionEdges.title: Pressure, Flow & Resistance
connectionEdges.link: Viscosity and diameter appear in both Poiseuille's law and the Reynolds number.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as the Reynolds number threshold for turbulence, which factors increase it (velocity, diameter, low viscosity in anemia), and where turbulence is found relative to a stenosis.

checkpoint.pearl: Re above 2000 = turbulence; found distal to a stenosis; anemia lowers viscosity and raises Re.
checkpoint.reflection: Why does anemia make turbulence more likely, and where along a stenosis would you look for it?

topics.title: Bernoulli & Continuity
topics.frontClue: Squeeze the hose: speed goes up, pressure goes down
topics.corePiece: The continuity equation states that volume flow is constant through a closed system: Q = A1 x v1 = A2 x v2. When cross-sectional area decreases at a stenosis, velocity increases proportionally, and when area widens distal to the narrowing, velocity falls again. Halving the area doubles the velocity. Bernoulli's principle is conservation of energy: total energy (pressure plus kinetic plus gravitational) stays constant along a streamline, so where velocity and kinetic energy increase, pressure energy decreases. Within a stenosis, velocity is highest and pressure is lowest, counterintuitive but correct. The simplified Bernoulli equation estimates the pressure gradient across a narrowing from the peak velocity: delta P = 4 x v squared, with v in m/s and delta P in mmHg; 3 m/s gives 36 mmHg. Distal to the stenosis pressure partly recovers, but energy lost to friction and turbulence is not regained. A stenosis becomes hemodynamically significant at about 50 percent diameter reduction, which equals about 75 percent area reduction, when distal flow and pressure begin to fall.
topics.whyLock: Combine the two laws: continuity predicts that velocity rises through a stenosis, and Bernoulli predicts that pressure falls there. That is why peak systolic velocity is the main Doppler criterion for grading stenosis. A classic trap is assuming pressure is highest inside the narrow segment; it is lowest. Another trap is the critical stenosis: a 50 percent diameter reduction equals roughly a 75 percent area reduction because area depends on radius squared. Expect calculations: if area falls to one third, velocity triples; if peak velocity is 4 m/s, the gradient is 64 mmHg.

connectionEdges.title: Pressure, Flow & Resistance
connectionEdges.link: Continuity is Q = v x A applied to a narrowing, keeping volume flow constant while velocity changes.

connectionEdges.title: Laminar vs Turbulent Flow
connectionEdges.link: The high-velocity jet created by continuity breaks into turbulence as it exits the stenosis.

connectionEdges.title: Doppler Equation & Angle
connectionEdges.link: Doppler measures the stenotic jet velocity that Bernoulli converts into a pressure gradient.

topics.registryApplication: Expect calculations using A1 x v1 = A2 x v2 or delta P = 4 x v squared, and questions asking where pressure is lowest (within the stenosis) or what diameter reduction is hemodynamically significant (50 percent).

checkpoint.pearl: Narrower means faster and lower pressure; delta P = 4 x v squared; 50 percent diameter = 75 percent area.
checkpoint.reflection: A jet measures 2.5 m/s. What is the estimated pressure gradient, and where in the vessel is pressure lowest?

topics.title: Venous Hemodynamics
topics.frontClue: Low pressure, huge capacity: breathing and gravity steer the veins
topics.corePiece: Veins form a low-pressure, high-capacitance system that holds about two thirds of the blood volume. Thin walls let them collapse at low pressure. Hydrostatic pressure is the weight of a column of blood: about 2 mmHg per inch (roughly 0.8 mmHg per cm) of height below the heart, zero at heart level, and negative above it. Standing raises ankle venous pressure to about 100 mmHg, while lying supine makes hydrostatic pressure in the legs essentially zero. Respiration produces phasicity. During inspiration the diaphragm descends, abdominal pressure rises, and thoracic pressure falls, so lower extremity venous flow decreases while upper extremity flow toward the heart increases. During expiration the pattern reverses and leg flow increases. A Valsalva maneuver stops leg venous outflow. The calf muscle pump compresses deep veins and valves prevent backflow; distal augmentation pushes blood toward the heart. Reflux longer than 0.5 seconds (1 second in the femoral and popliteal veins) suggests valvular incompetence, and continuous non-phasic flow suggests a more proximal obstruction.
topics.whyLock: Reason with pressure gradients: venous return increases when pressure near the heart falls or pressure in the limb rises. Inspiration raises abdominal pressure, compressing the IVC and reducing leg return; expiration releases it. The hydrostatic principle explains why leg reflux testing is done standing or in reverse Trendelenburg, which distends the veins. Traps: assuming inspiration increases venous flow everywhere (it decreases leg flow and increases arm flow), and forgetting that hydrostatic pressure is zero at the level of the heart. Loss of respiratory phasicity in a common femoral vein points to obstruction proximal to it, closer to the heart, such as iliac vein thrombosis.

connectionEdges.title: Pressure, Flow & Resistance
connectionEdges.link: Venous flow, like arterial flow, follows pressure gradients set by gravity, respiration, and the muscle pump.

connectionEdges.title: Bernoulli & Continuity
connectionEdges.link: Gravitational energy is one of the three energy terms in Bernoulli's principle and dominates venous pressure when standing.

connectionEdges.title: Spectral Analysis
connectionEdges.link: Phasicity, augmentation, and reflux duration are all read from the venous spectral waveform.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as how respiration affects leg versus arm venous flow, how to calculate hydrostatic pressure, or what loss of phasicity or reflux duration implies.

checkpoint.pearl: Inspiration: leg venous flow down, arm flow up. Hydrostatic pressure about 2 mmHg per inch below the heart.
checkpoint.reflection: Why does lower extremity venous flow decrease during inspiration while upper extremity flow increases?

topics.title: Thermal Bioeffects & TI
topics.frontClue: Bone soaks up heat; TI estimates how many degrees you might add
topics.corePiece: Thermal bioeffects result from absorption, the conversion of sound energy into heat. Heating increases with intensity, exposure time, frequency (higher frequencies are absorbed more), and the absorption properties of the tissue: bone absorbs the most, soft tissue less, and fluid the least. The thermal index (TI) is the ratio of the acoustic power being transmitted to the power needed to raise tissue temperature by 1 degree Celsius, so a TI of 2 suggests a possible rise of about 2 degrees under worst-case assumptions. It is an estimate, not a measurement. TIS applies to soft tissue, TIB to bone at or near the focus (second and third trimester fetal imaging), and TIC to cranial bone at the surface. AIUM statements note no confirmed adverse effects from a temperature rise of 2 degrees C or less above normal, while fetal temperatures of 41 degrees C or higher sustained for several minutes are considered potentially hazardous. PW Doppler, with a stationary, focused beam, has the greatest heating potential; B-mode the least.
topics.whyLock: TI is a relative guide on the display, so keep it as low as reasonably achievable and limit dwell time, especially in obstetric, neonatal, and ophthalmic exams. Trap: assuming a higher frequency is always safer; it is absorbed more, increasing heating near the surface even though it reduces mechanical risk. Another trap: assuming Doppler is harmless because it is used briefly; spectral Doppler over ossified fetal bone produces the highest temperature rise. Well-perfused tissue heats less, and a febrile patient has less margin. Answer TIB for fetal bone, TIC for skull at the surface, and TIS for soft tissue.

connectionEdges.title: Attenuation
connectionEdges.link: Absorption, one component of attenuation, is the mechanism that converts acoustic energy into heat.

connectionEdges.title: Mechanical Bioeffects & MI
connectionEdges.link: TI addresses heating while MI addresses cavitation; the two respond to frequency in opposite directions.

connectionEdges.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
connectionEdges.link: SPTA intensity is most closely tied to heating and is limited under ALARA.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on which TI applies to a given exam (TIB for fetal bone), what TI represents, and which tissue or mode carries the most heating risk.

checkpoint.pearl: TI 1 = possible 1 degree C rise; bone absorbs most; PW Doppler heats most; TIS, TIB, TIC.
checkpoint.reflection: Which thermal index should you watch during a third trimester fetal Doppler exam, and why?

topics.title: Mechanical Bioeffects & MI
topics.frontClue: Bubbles swell, shrink, and sometimes burst: MI rates the risk
topics.corePiece: Mechanical bioeffects arise from the pressure variations of the wave itself, chiefly through cavitation, the interaction of sound with gas bubbles. In stable cavitation, microbubbles oscillate (expand and contract) without bursting, which can cause microstreaming, shear stress on nearby cells. In transient (inertial, normal) cavitation, bubbles expand rapidly and collapse violently, producing very high local temperatures and pressures, shock waves, and free radicals; it is the more dangerous form. The mechanical index (MI) estimates the likelihood of cavitation: MI = peak rarefactional pressure (MPa) / square root of frequency (MHz). MI rises with a higher peak rarefactional (negative) pressure and with a lower frequency. The FDA limit for diagnostic imaging is an MI of 1.9. Tissues that contain gas, such as lung and bowel, are most vulnerable, and lung hemorrhage in animals is a documented mechanical effect. Contrast agents introduce bubbles and therefore increase cavitation potential; low-MI imaging, often below about 0.3, preserves microbubbles, while high-MI pulses deliberately destroy them.
topics.whyLock: Remember the two parts of the formula: pressure on top, frequency under a square root on the bottom. Lower frequency therefore raises MI and cavitation risk, the opposite of the thermal story, where higher frequency increases absorption and heating. That inversion is a favorite exam contrast. MI depends on peak rarefactional pressure, not compressional pressure, because bubbles grow during rarefaction. Trap: mixing up stable and transient cavitation; stable is oscillation without collapse, transient is violent collapse. If a question mentions contrast agents and bubble destruction, think of MI, not TI.

connectionEdges.title: Thermal Bioeffects & TI
connectionEdges.link: TI and MI are the two on-screen safety indices; heating rises with frequency while MI falls with frequency.

connectionEdges.title: Harmonic Imaging & Contrast Agents
connectionEdges.link: Microbubble contrast is imaged at low MI to avoid bubble destruction and raises cavitation potential.

connectionEdges.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
connectionEdges.link: Lowering output power reduces peak rarefactional pressure and therefore MI, in keeping with ALARA.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as the MI formula and how it changes with frequency or pressure, the difference between stable and transient cavitation, and which tissues are most susceptible.

checkpoint.pearl: MI = peak rarefactional pressure / square root of frequency; low frequency and gas raise the risk.
checkpoint.reflection: If frequency increases from 2 MHz to 8 MHz at the same peak rarefactional pressure, what happens to the MI?

topics.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
topics.frontClue: Raise gain before power, and scan only as long as you need to
topics.corePiece: ALARA, as low as reasonably achievable, is the guiding principle of ultrasound safety: obtain the diagnostic information with the lowest exposure. In practice, minimize exam time, increase receiver gain before output power, monitor TI and MI, and limit Doppler over the fetus or eye. Intensity (power divided by area, in W/cm2 or mW/cm2) is reported in several forms depending on where and when it is measured: spatial peak (SP) or spatial average (SA), combined with temporal peak (TP), pulse average (PA), or temporal average (TA). SPTP is the highest value and SATA the lowest. SPTA is most closely linked to tissue heating and is the intensity most often tested; the FDA limit for derated SPTA is 720 mW/cm2 for most applications. Older AIUM statements noted no confirmed bioeffects in mammalian tissue for SPTA below 100 mW/cm2 with unfocused beams or 1 W/cm2 with focused beams. Temporal average equals pulse average times duty factor, and the beam uniformity coefficient (SP / SA) links the spatial values.
topics.whyLock: For intensities, remember the extremes: SPTP is the largest, SATA the smallest, and SPTA the one tied to thermal bioeffects. Temporal peak and pulse average values exceed the temporal average because a pulsed transducer is silent most of the time (low duty factor). For continuous wave, the duty factor is 1, so pulse average and temporal average are equal. The ALARA trap: when the image is too dark, the safest first move is to increase receiver gain, which amplifies returning echoes without increasing patient exposure; raising output power increases both the signal and the exposure. The operator, not the machine, is responsible for ALARA.

connectionEdges.title: Output Power vs Receiver Gain
connectionEdges.link: ALARA favors raising receiver gain first because gain does not change patient exposure.

connectionEdges.title: Duty Factor
connectionEdges.link: Temporal average intensity equals pulse average intensity times the duty factor.

connectionEdges.title: Thermal Bioeffects & TI
connectionEdges.link: SPTA, the intensity limited by the FDA at 720 mW/cm2, is the one most relevant to heating.

topics.registryApplication: Expect questions on the first step to brighten an image (increase receiver gain), the ranking of intensities (SPTP highest, SATA lowest), and which intensity relates to heating (SPTA).

checkpoint.pearl: Gain before power; SPTP highest, SATA lowest, SPTA heats.

topics.title: Quality Assurance & Phantoms
topics.frontClue: Test the machine on fake tissue before it fools you on real tissue
topics.corePiece: Quality assurance (QA) is routine, documented testing that confirms an ultrasound system performs accurately and consistently. Phantoms are test objects with known dimensions and properties. The AIUM 100 mm test object contains stainless steel rods in a medium with a propagation speed of 1540 m/s; it tests axial resolution, lateral resolution, dead zone, registration, and range (depth) accuracy, but it has no tissue texture and cannot evaluate gray scale. Tissue-mimicking phantoms have attenuation and speed similar to soft tissue and contain nylon fibers, simulated cysts, and masses; they test the same items plus sensitivity, penetration, uniformity, and contrast or gray-scale resolution. Doppler phantoms, using a moving string or a pump with blood-mimicking fluid, test velocity accuracy, sample volume location, Doppler penetration, and direction. Hydrophones are small piezoelectric needle or membrane probes that measure acoustic output: pressure amplitude, period, and pulse timing, from which intensity is calculated. The dead zone is the region nearest the transducer where imaging is unreliable, and registration is the accurate placement of echoes.
topics.whyLock: QA questions usually ask which device tests a given parameter. Match parameter to tool: resolution and range accuracy on the AIUM test object or a tissue phantom; gray scale, contrast, and cyst detection only on a tissue-mimicking phantom; velocity accuracy on a Doppler phantom; acoustic output on a hydrophone. Trap: the AIUM test object cannot evaluate gray scale because it lacks tissue-like scatterers. The dead zone becomes smaller with higher frequency transducers and shorter pulses. QA should be scheduled and logged, and results are compared against a baseline recorded when the system was new or serviced.

connectionEdges.title: Axial Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Pin groups at decreasing spacing in a test object measure axial resolution directly.

connectionEdges.title: Lateral & Elevational Resolution
connectionEdges.link: Lateral resolution is checked with pins lying side by side at the same depth.

connectionEdges.title: ALARA & Acoustic Intensities
connectionEdges.link: Hydrophones measure the pressures and intensities that safety limits and ALARA are based on.

topics.registryApplication: Typically asked as which phantom or device tests a specific parameter, for example gray scale (tissue-mimicking phantom), velocity accuracy (Doppler phantom), or acoustic output (hydrophone).

checkpoint.pearl: AIUM object: resolution and accuracy, no gray scale. Tissue phantom: adds gray scale. Hydrophone: output.

topics.title: Sensitivity, Specificity & Predictive Values
topics.frontClue: SnNout and SpPin: sensitive tests rule out, specific tests rule in
topics.corePiece: Test statistics compare ultrasound with a gold standard (angiography, surgery, pathology) in a 2 x 2 table. A true positive (TP) is a positive test with disease present; a false positive (FP) is a positive test with no disease; a true negative (TN) is a negative test with no disease; and a false negative (FN) is a negative test with disease present. Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN): the ability to detect disease when it is present. Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): the ability to call normals normal. Positive predictive value (PPV) = TP / (TP + FP): when the test is positive, how often it is right. Negative predictive value (NPV) = TN / (TN + FN): when the test is negative, how often it is right. Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all tests. Sensitivity and specificity describe the test and do not change with disease prevalence, while PPV rises and NPV falls as prevalence increases. Lowering a threshold raises sensitivity but lowers specificity.
topics.whyLock: The quickest way to avoid errors is to look at the denominator. Sensitivity and specificity divide by what the gold standard says (all diseased or all normal patients); predictive values divide by what the test says (all positives or all negatives). Accuracy is all correct results over all patients. Worked example: 90 TP, 10 FN, 80 TN, and 20 FP give sensitivity 90 percent, specificity 80 percent, PPV 82 percent, NPV 89 percent, and accuracy 85 percent. Trap: swapping false positives and false negatives. A false negative is a missed disease; a false positive is a false alarm.

connectionEdges.title: Quality Assurance & Phantoms
connectionEdges.link: Both verify accuracy: QA checks the machine, while test statistics check how well the exam matches the truth.

connectionEdges.title: Bernoulli & Continuity
connectionEdges.link: Velocity criteria for grading stenosis are validated against angiography, and moving the threshold trades sensitivity for specificity.

topics.registryApplication: Expect a 2 x 2 table with counts and a request to calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, or accuracy, often with a false positive or false negative distractor.

checkpoint.pearl: Sensitivity and specificity divide by the truth; predictive values divide by the test result.
